name: OpenFEC API
description: Every federal campaign-finance filing the FEC holds, as JSON: candidates and committees, receipts and disbursements down to the individual contribution, independent expenditures, electioneering communications, and the filings themselves. Schedule A alone runs to hundreds of millions of itemised contributions with donor name, employer, occupation, city and ZIP. This is the primary source that ProPublica's campaign-finance API was reformatting, and unlike that one it is alive, free and unrestricted.
geography: US federal elections; contributions carry contributor city, state and ZIP

temporal.start: 1979-1980 cycle for itemised data; some committee records earlier
temporal.grain: per filing and per itemised transaction
temporal.updated: continuously as filings arrive; quarterly and monthly reporting deadlines drive the volume

license.name: US government work, public domain
license.redistribution: unrestricted for analysis and republication, with one statutory exception: contributor information may not be sold or used for soliciting contributions or for commercial purposes. That is federal law (52 U.S.C. 30111(a)(4)), not a licence term.

access.auth_note: Free key from https://api.data.gov/signup/ -- the same key as Congress.gov and every other api.data.gov federal API. DEMO_KEY works for exploring, at 10 requests/hour.
access.size_hint: an API page is tens of KB; the bulk itemised-contributions file for one cycle is several GB
access.rate_limit: 1,000 requests per hour with a registered key; DEMO_KEY capped at 10/hour (X-Ratelimit-Limit: 10, observed 2026-09-10)
access.pagination: per_page up to 100 with page for small result sets; Schedule A and B require keyset paging via last_index and last_contribution_receipt_date

probes.description: Candidate list, with the public DEMO_KEY
probes.note: DEMO_KEY's 10/hour budget is shared per IP across every api.data.gov API. A 429 here means that budget is spent, not that the FEC is down -- probe.py classifies it as throttled.

probes.description: Itemised contributions with no filter -- documents the required-parameter gate
probes.note: A deliberate 400. Schedule A refuses an unfiltered query rather than starting to stream 400 million rows, and the error names every filter it will accept. Verified 2026-09-10.

recipes.title: Find a candidate, then their committee totals
Itemised contributions to one committee, keyset-paged
recipes.code:
U="https://api.open.fec.gov/v1/schedules/schedule_a/?api_key=$FEC_API_KEY&committee_id=C00401224&two_year_transaction_period=2024&per_page=100"
curl -s "$U" -o p1.json
# take last_indexes from the response and feed them back -- do NOT increment page
python3 -c "import json; p=json.load(open('p1.json'))['pagination']['last_indexes']; print(p)"

gotchas.trap: Schedule A and Schedule B refuse to page with page=N past the first few pages, and the fix is not more pages -- it is a different paging mechanism entirely.
gotchas.fix: Use keyset pagination: read pagination.last_indexes from each response and pass its members (last_index, last_contribution_receipt_date) as query parameters on the next call. Incrementing `page` silently returns wrong or repeated rows on these two endpoints while working fine on every other one, which is why it takes so long to notice.

gotchas.trap: An unfiltered Schedule A query returns 400, not data, and the message is easy to read as a malformed request.
gotchas.fix: It is telling you what it needs. Supply two_year_transaction_period, or one of committee_id, contributor_id, contributor_name, contributor_city, contributor_zip, contributor_employer, contributor_occupation or image_number. Verified 2026-09-10.

gotchas.trap: Contributions are itemised only above a threshold, so small-dollar giving is invisible at the transaction level -- and the threshold has changed over time.
gotchas.fix: Use the committee totals endpoints for unitemised sums. An analysis of 'who gave' built only on Schedule A systematically over-represents large donors, which is a finding about the data rather than about donors.

gotchas.trap: The same person appears as many contributor strings -- 'SMITH, JOHN', 'Smith, John A.', 'JOHN SMITH' -- with employer and occupation self-reported and frequently blank or 'NONE'.
gotchas.fix: There is no donor id. Any per-person aggregation is a record-linkage problem you have to solve and should disclose. contributor_id exists only for committee-to-committee transfers.

gotchas.trap: Amendments. A committee refiles a report and both the original and the amendment are in the data, so summing naively double-counts.
gotchas.fix: Filter on is_individual and prefer the endpoints that already deduplicate (the totals and by_* aggregates) when you want a sum rather than a transaction list.

gotchas.trap: 'Cycle' and 'two_year_transaction_period' look interchangeable and are not.
gotchas.fix: two_year_transaction_period is the two-year window the transaction falls in; cycle is the election cycle the committee is filing for. A Senate candidate runs on a six-year cycle and their filings span three two-year periods.

fields: candidate_id -- H/S/P prefix plus state and number, e.g. S2MA00170
committee_id -- C followed by 8 digits; the join key for almost everything
two_year_transaction_period -- required on Schedule A; not the same as cycle
pagination.last_indexes -- the keyset cursor for Schedules A and B
contributor_employer / contributor_occupation -- self-reported, often blank, never normalised
is_individual -- separates individual contributions from transfers and refunds
